steps.title: Why atoms bond
steps.body: Atoms react to get a **full outer shell**, like the noble gases. Metals in Groups 1 and 2 have one or two outer electrons and **lose** them. Non-metals in Groups 6 and 7 are one or two short and **gain** them. Losing or gaining electrons turns an atom into an **ion**, a charged particle.

steps.text: Left with 2,8, a full outer shell
It is now Na⁺: 11 protons, 10 electrons, charge 1+

check.prompt: Which atom will lose electrons when it forms an ion?
check.solution: Magnesium has two outer electrons to lose. Oxygen and fluorine gain; neon already has a full shell.

steps.title: Forming ions: sodium chloride
steps.body: Sodium gives its outer electron to chlorine. Sodium becomes **Na⁺** (2,8) and chlorine becomes **Cl⁻** (2,8,8). The dot-and-cross diagram shows the outer shells only, with the transferred electron drawn as a cross among the dots.

visuals.alt: Dot-and-cross diagram for sodium chloride: sodium loses one electron to chlorine, giving Na+ and Cl-

check.prompt: What is the charge on a magnesium ion?
check.solution: Magnesium, 2,8,2, loses two electrons: 12 protons, 10 electrons, charge 2+.

steps.title: Magnesium oxide: two electrons move
steps.body: Group 2 metals lose two electrons and Group 6 non-metals gain two, so both ions carry a charge of 2.

visuals.alt: Dot-and-cross diagram for magnesium oxide: magnesium loses two electrons to oxygen, giving Mg 2+ and O 2-

check.prompt: Which compound has ions with charges 2+ and 1−?
check.solution: Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻. Two chloride ions are needed per magnesium ion: MgCl₂.

steps.title: The ionic bond and the lattice
steps.body: An **ionic bond** is the strong **electrostatic attraction** between oppositely charged ions. The ions do not pair up: every positive ion is surrounded by negative ions and every negative by positives, in a regular repeating pattern called a **giant ionic lattice**. The forces act in **all directions**.

visuals.alt: A giant ionic lattice: alternating positive and negative ions in a regular grid

check.prompt: What holds the ions together in sodium chloride?
check.solution: Electrostatic attraction between the opposite charges. Shared electrons are covalent; the sea of electrons is metallic.

markScheme.description: Electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions

options: Strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions

steps.title: Formulae from charges
steps.body: The charges in a compound must **cancel**. Magnesium chloride: Mg²⁺ needs two Cl⁻, so **MgCl₂**. Aluminium oxide: Al³⁺ and O²⁻; the lowest common multiple of 3 and 2 is 6, so two Al³⁺ and three O²⁻: **Al₂O₃**. Swap the charge numbers over and drop the signs.

check.prompt: Write the formula of the compound formed from Al³⁺ and O²⁻.
check.solution: Two Al³⁺ (6+) balance three O²⁻ (6−): Al₂O₃.

steps.title: Properties of ionic compounds
steps.body:
- **High melting and boiling points**: many strong electrostatic forces to overcome in all directions, so a lot of energy is needed.
- **Do not conduct when solid**: the ions are fixed in the lattice.
- **Conduct when molten or dissolved in water**: the lattice breaks down and the ions are free to move and carry charge.
- Many dissolve in water.

steps.text: Solid NaCl: ions locked in place, no
Molten NaCl: ions free to move, yes
NaCl solution: ions free to move, yes

check.prompt: Why does molten sodium chloride conduct electricity?
check.solution: In an ionic compound the charge carriers are the ions, and they can only move once the lattice has melted.
options: The ions are free to move
The electrons are free to move
The atoms are free to move

steps.title: Your turn: explain in mark-scheme language
steps.body: Exam explanations follow a shape: **structure, forces, energy**. Name the structure (giant ionic lattice), name the forces (strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, in all directions), then say what that means for energy (a lot needed to overcome them). Practise saying it out loud.

visuals.problem: Why does magnesium oxide have a high melting point?

steps.text: Strong electrostatic forces between Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions, in all directions
Lots of energy needed to overcome them
So the melting point is high

check.prompt: Which phrase would an examiner reject in an explanation of melting point?
check.solution: "The bonds are strong" does not say what kind of bonds or between what. The other three are mark-scheme phrases.
options: Strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions
A lot of energy is needed to overcome the forces
The forces act in all directions

steps.title: Grade 9: comparing compounds, and the limits of the model
steps.body:
Magnesium oxide melts at 2852 °C, sodium chloride at 801 °C. Both are ionic, so the difference is in the **ions**: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry twice the charge of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ and are smaller, so the electrostatic attraction is stronger and more energy is needed.

Top questions also ask about **models**. A dot-and-cross diagram shows electron transfer but not the lattice. A ball-and-stick model shows the lattice but exaggerates the gaps and shows "sticks" where there are no bonds. A space-filling model shows the packing but hides the ions inside.

visuals.alt: A giant ionic lattice with alternating charges, the arrangement no dot-and-cross diagram can show

check.prompt: Which factor makes the attraction between ions in magnesium oxide stronger than in sodium chloride?
check.solution: 2+ and 2− against 1+ and 1−: double the charge, and the ions are smaller too.
options: The ions carry a greater charge

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Metals lose electrons to form positive ions; non-metals gain to form negative ions. Group number tells you the charge.
- Ionic bond: strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, in a giant lattice.
- Formulae: charges must cancel. MgCl₂, Al₂O₃.
- High melting points; conduct only when molten or dissolved, because ions must be free to move.
- Bigger charges and smaller ions mean stronger attraction.

questions.solution: Metals lose electrons to become positive ions; non-metals gain them to become negative ions. The opposite charges attract.
options: a metal and a noble gas

questions.prompt: What is the charge on a sodium ion?
questions.solution: Sodium is in Group 1, so it loses one electron and becomes Na⁺, with a charge of 1+.

questions.prompt: A chlorine atom has the electronic structure 2,8,7. What is the electronic structure of a chloride ion, Cl⁻?
questions.solution: A chloride ion has gained one electron, filling the outer shell: 2,8,8, the same as argon.

questions.prompt: Write the formula of calcium chloride. Calcium forms Ca²⁺ ions and chlorine forms Cl⁻ ions.
questions.solution: The charges must cancel: one 2+ needs two 1−. $\text{CaCl}_2$.

markScheme.description: Two chloride ions needed to balance 2+

questions.prompt: Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct electricity?
questions.solution: The ions are there, but locked in the lattice. Conduction needs charged particles that can move, which happens when the compound is molten or dissolved.

markScheme.description: Ions cannot move in the solid

options: The ions are held in fixed positions and cannot move
It has no ions until it is dissolved

questions.prompt: Explain why sodium chloride has a high melting point.
questions.solution: Four ideas in mark-scheme language: giant lattice, strong electrostatic forces, between oppositely charged ions in all directions, lots of energy to overcome. "Bonds" alone is not enough; say what kind.

markScheme.description: Strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions
In all directions throughout the lattice

criteria.text: Sodium chloride is a giant ionic lattice
Held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions
These forces act in all directions throughout the lattice, so there are many to overcome
A large amount of energy is needed to break them

questions.modelAnswer: Sodium chloride has a giant ionic lattice structure. The oppositely charged sodium and chloride ions are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction, which act in all directions throughout the lattice. A large amount of energy is needed to overcome these many strong forces, so the melting point is high.

questions.prompt: Write the formula of aluminium oxide. Aluminium forms Al³⁺ ions and oxygen forms O²⁻ ions.
questions.solution: Two Al³⁺ give 6+, three O²⁻ give 6−. $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$.

questions.prompt: In the dot-and-cross diagram for magnesium oxide, how many electrons move from the magnesium atom to the oxygen atom?
questions.solution: Magnesium is 2,8,2 and loses both outer electrons; oxygen is 2,6 and gains two.

visual.alt: Dot-and-cross diagram: magnesium loses two electrons to oxygen, giving Mg 2+ and O 2- ions

questions.prompt: Magnesium oxide melts at 2852 °C and sodium chloride melts at 801 °C. Both are ionic compounds. Explain the difference in melting points.
questions.solution: Level-marked. Level 3 compares both compounds, names the ions with charges, links charge and size to the strength of attraction, and ends with the energy conclusion.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two relevant points about the two lattices, ion charges, attraction strength, and energy, not linked
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a mostly correct account of the two lattices, ion charges, attraction strength, and energy with some links
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, complete comparison of the two lattices, ion charges, attraction strength, and energy using the correct terms

criteria.text: Both are giant ionic lattices with electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions
Magnesium oxide contains Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions; sodium chloride contains Na⁺ and Cl⁻
The 2+ and 2− ions have a greater charge, so the electrostatic attraction between them is stronger
Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ are also smaller than Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so the ions are closer together, which strengthens the attraction further
More energy is needed to overcome the stronger forces in magnesium oxide
Therefore magnesium oxide has the higher melting point

questions.modelAnswer: Both compounds are giant ionic lattices in which oppositely charged ions are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction. Magnesium oxide is made of Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions, whereas sodium chloride is made of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. The ions in magnesium oxide carry twice the charge, so the electrostatic attraction between them is much stronger. They are also smaller, so the charges are closer together, which strengthens the attraction further. More energy is needed to overcome the forces in magnesium oxide, so its melting point is higher.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a limitation of a dot-and-cross diagram of sodium chloride?
questions.solution: A dot-and-cross diagram shows one pair of ions and the electron transfer. It says nothing about the lattice, the relative sizes of ions, or the fact that each ion is surrounded by several others.
options: It does not show that the ions form a giant three-dimensional lattice
It does not show which electrons are transferred
It does not show the charges on the ions

questions.prompt: Element X forms a compound with the formula X₂SO₄. The sulfate ion is SO₄²⁻. What is the charge on an X ion?
questions.solution: One sulfate ion carries 2−, so two X ions must carry 2+ between them: each X ion is 1+.

markScheme.description: 2− must be balanced by two X ions

questions.prompt: A metal M forms M³⁺ ions. In its oxide, how many oxide ions, O²⁻, are there for every two M³⁺ ions?
questions.solution: Two M³⁺ carry 6+. Each O²⁻ carries 2−, so three are needed for 6−: $\text{M}_2\text{O}_3$.

questions.prompt: Explain why potassium bromide conducts electricity when it is molten but not when it is solid.
questions.solution: Say ions, not electrons: ionic compounds never conduct by electrons moving.

criteria.text: Potassium bromide contains K⁺ and Br⁻ ions
In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice by strong electrostatic forces and cannot move
When molten the lattice has broken down and the ions are free to move
Conduction needs charged particles that can move and carry the charge, so only the molten compound conducts

questions.modelAnswer: Potassium bromide is made of K⁺ and Br⁻ ions. In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in a giant lattice by strong electrostatic forces, so they cannot move. When the compound is molten, the lattice has broken down and the ions are free to move. Electrical conduction needs charged particles that are free to move and carry the charge through the substance, so only the molten compound conducts.

questions.prompt: Which pair of ions both have the same electronic structure as neon, 2,8?
questions.solution: Na (2,8,1) loses one electron: 2,8. F (2,7) gains one: 2,8. Cl⁻, K⁺ and S²⁻ are all 2,8,8, like argon.

examTechnique.body: Ionic bonding questions range from one-mark formulae to six-mark explanations. The explanation marks are for specific phrases: giant ionic lattice, strong electrostatic forces of attraction, oppositely charged ions, in all directions, lots of energy to overcome. Dot-and-cross diagrams need the outer shell only, square brackets round each ion, and the charge outside the bracket.
examinerErrors: Saying ionic compounds conduct because electrons move. It is the ions.
Writing "strong bonds" without saying electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions.
Drawing all the electrons, or drawing the transferred electron as the wrong symbol.
Getting a formula wrong by matching one ion to one ion regardless of charge, such as MgCl.
Saying molecules of sodium chloride. Ionic compounds have no molecules.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer names the structure, the particles, and the forces in the right words every time, compares compounds by ion charge and size, writes formulae from charges without hesitation, and can say what each model of a lattice leaves out.
